newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK politicians draw battle lines on Social Chapter.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK politicians draw battle lines on Social Chapter.

text.p: Opposition Labour Party finance spokesman Gordon Brown said on Monday a Labour government would sign up to the EU's Social Chapter but would resist an expansion of majority voting on social issues.
Brown also told the Confederation of British Industry's annual conference that a Labour government would have a target for low and stable inflation and would deliver on it.
"We will not be satisfied with simply talking as tough as the Tories. We plan to deliver," he said.
The government has a target for underlying inflation of 2.5 percent, a level an advisor to Brown said was a sensible aim. Underlying inflation was 2.9 percent year-on-year in September.
But with the proposed 1999 start date for a single European currency looming, it was Europe that dominated the CBI stage.

Brown said in order to ensure Britain was heard on social issues in the European Union, a Labour government would sign up for the Social Chapter, which guarantees minimum work rights. But he added: "Not only do we have no plans to extend qualified majority voting...but we will veto any attempt to do so."
Taking up the cudgels for the government, defence secretary Michael Portillo told top industry delegates that the Social Chapter was "a catalogue of job-destroying measures."
Portillo said Brown's commitment was an empty one. "Labour is committed to joining the Social Chapter. That is in itself a massive extension of majority voting," he said.

Most of the captains of industry gathered at the CBI's conference appeared to share Portillo's concerns. A survey of nearly 1,700 firms released by the CBI and the British Chambers of Commerce on the eve of the conference showed 73 percent thought Britain should keep its opt-out from the Social Chapter.
Andrew Buxton, chairman of Barclays Bank and the CBI's economic affairs committee, agreed the opt-out should be kept but said the Chapter as it stands contains nothing too harmful.
However, once involved, Britain could become loaded with further legislation voted through by the majority of EU members.

Portillo added that the Labour Party would accept an EU working directive which states that no-one should have to work longer than 48 hours a week. "That would restrict what families could earn, make us uncompetitive and cost jobs."

Deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine also waded into the debate in the northern spa town of Harrogate. He said Prime Minister John Major would fight to keep the directive from being implemented in Britain even if a European Court of Justice decision, due on Tuesday, went against the government.
For the pro-European camp Leon Brittan, vice-president of the European Commission said it would be hard for Britain to persuade its EU partners to allow it exemption from the working directive.

Brittan also said European Economic and Monetary Union was on course. "Don't believe those who say that EMU cannot happen by the end of the century," he said. But Heseltine, his former Conservative colleague, thought a 1999 start date for a single currency was "very unlikely".

The other workplace issue to loom large on the first day of the CBI conference was that of a minimum wage. A Labour government would introduce one at an unspecified level while Heseltine pledged that Conservatives would always resist one.
Buxton at the CBI said his organisation disagreed with the idea in principle but said if one was established, the level would be more crucial than the principle.
"There is absolutely no doubt that at 4.26 pounds, jobs would be lost. But at 3.50, fewer jobs would go." The Trades Union Congress has called for a minimum wage of 4.26 pounds.
